mainTopic: Humility (רבי אלעזר and the ugly man), which collapsing walls call for a fast, and the merits and good deeds of רב אדא בר אהבה and רב הונא.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a story. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון insults a very ugly man, who answers, 'Go tell the Craftsman who made me.' רבי אלעזר begs forgiveness, and the man forgives him only when the townspeople ask. רבי אלעזר then teaches that a person should be soft like a reed, not stiff like a cedar. Next the גמרא returns to the משנה and explains that a fast is called only when sturdy walls collapse, not walls that were ready to fall because they were weak, very tall, or standing on a riverbank. Stories about weak walls follow, showing how the great merit of רב אדא בר אהבה protected others. רבי ינאי warns never to rely on a miracle, since a miracle is deducted from one's merits. The גמרא then lists רב אדא בר אהבה's lifelong habits and the generous deeds of רב הונא: fixing dangerous walls, buying leftover vegetables before שבת, sharing medicine, and opening his doors at meals. The amud ends as רבא says he can follow all of these habits except one; his explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר insults an ugly man
steps.stepSummary: A very ugly man greets רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון. The רבי does not greet him back and insults his looks instead.
steps.simpleTranslation: He met a very ugly man. The man said, 'Peace be upon you, my teacher!' He did not answer the greeting. Instead he said: 'Empty one, how ugly that man is! Is everyone in your city as ugly as you?'
steps.whatsHappening: The story goes on: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון meets a very ugly man, ignores his friendly greeting, and mocks his appearance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man was polite and respectful, calling him 'רבי'. The response was cold and insulting. This sets up the whole lesson: a great Torah scholar slipped into arrogance and hurt someone with words.

phrases.english: He happened upon a certain person
who was exceedingly ugly.
He said to him: Greetings to you, my rabbi!
But he did not return his greeting.
phrases.notes: 'He' here is רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון, the main character of this story.

phrases.english: He said to him: Worthless one,
how ugly is that man!
phrases.notes: 'That man' is an indirect way of saying 'you'. He is really insulting the person in front of him.

phrases.english: Are perhaps all the people of your city
as ugly as you?

steps.triggerLanguage: נִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ אָדָם אֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה מְכוֹעָר בְּיוֹתֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a story that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A great scholar insulted a man for his looks, which sets up a lesson in humility.

steps.title: The man's sharp reply about his Maker
steps.stepSummary: The man answers: go complain to the Craftsman who made me.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'I don't know. But go and tell the Craftsman who made me, "How ugly is this vessel that You made."'
steps.whatsHappening: The insulted man answers with a powerful point: mocking how someone looks is really criticizing ה׳, who created him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not answer the question about his city. Instead he changes the focus. A person did not make his own face, so an insult about looks is aimed at the Creator. This line shows רבי אלעזר what he did wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: craftsman; here it refers to ה׳, the Creator
vessel, a made object; here the man calls himself a 'vessel'

phrases.english: He said to him: I do not know,
but go and say to the Craftsman Who made me:
"How ugly is this vessel that You made."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ, אֶלָּא לֵךְ וֶאֱמוֹר לָאוּמָּן שֶׁעֲשָׂאַנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the insulting question in step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Insulting someone's looks is really insulting the Creator who made him.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר begs forgiveness and is refused
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר realizes his sin, bows down, and asks forgiveness. The man refuses unless he goes and says the insult to the Creator.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once he realized he had sinned, he got off his donkey, bowed down before the man, and said, 'I wronged you, forgive me!' The man said, 'I won't forgive you until you go to the Craftsman who made me and say, "How ugly is this vessel You made."'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר admits his mistake right away and humbles himself completely. The man still refuses to forgive him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The quick change is important: getting off the donkey and lying on the ground is the opposite of the pride he showed a moment ago. The man's refusal repeats his point. The impossible condition shows how serious the insult was.

keyTerms.meaning: lay down flat, bowed fully on the ground
I have wronged you (literally, I have been humbled before you)

phrases.english: Once he himself realized that he had sinned,
he got down from the donkey
and lay flat on the ground before him,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר לוֹ: נַעֲנֵיתִי לְךָ, מְחוֹל לִי!
phrases.english: and said to him: I have wronged you, forgive me!
He said to him: I will not forgive you
until you go to the Craftsman Who made me

phrases.aramaic: וֶאֱמוֹר לוֹ: כַּמָּה מְכוֹעָר כְּלִי זֶה שֶׁעָשִׂיתָ.
phrases.english: and say to Him: How ugly is this vessel that You made.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן שֶׁיָּדַע בְּעַצְמוֹ שֶׁחָטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows רבי אלעזר's reaction to the man's reply in step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He sincerely asks forgiveness, but the man refuses.

steps.title: The townspeople ask the man to forgive
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר follows the man to town. The people greet רבי אלעזר with honor, the man tells them what happened, and they ask him to forgive because רבי אלעזר is a great Torah scholar.
steps.simpleTranslation: He walked behind the man until they reached his city. The townspeople came out and called, 'Peace to you, my rabbi, my rabbi, my master, my master!' The man asked, 'Who are you calling rabbi?' They said, 'The one walking behind you.' He said, 'If this is a rabbi, may there not be many like him in Israel!' They asked why. He told them what had happened. They said, 'Even so, forgive him, because he is a great Torah scholar.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר keeps following the man to try to make peace. When they reach town, the people's honor for him leads the man to tell everyone what happened.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man's sharp line 'may there not be many like him' shows that he is still hurt. The townspeople do not deny what happened. Instead they ask for forgiveness for the sake of the honor of Torah.

keyTerms.meaning: great in Torah, a major Torah scholar

phrases.english: He walked behind him
until he reached his city.
The people of his city came out to greet him,
and they were saying to him:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁלוֹם עָלֶיךָ רַבִּי רַבִּי, מוֹרִי מוֹרִי!
phrases.english: Greetings to you, my rabbi, my rabbi, my master, my master!

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: לְמִי אַתֶּם קוֹרִין רַבִּי רַבִּי?
phrases.english: He said to them: Whom are you calling 'my rabbi, my rabbi'?
They said to him: This one, who is walking behind you.
He said to them: If this one is a rabbi,
may there not be many like him in Israel.
They said to him: Why?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: כָּךְ וְכָךְ עָשָׂה לִי.
phrases.english: He said to them: He did such and such to me.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אַף עַל פִּי כֵּן, מְחוֹל לוֹ,
phrases.english: They said to him: Even so, forgive him,
for he is a man great in Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה מְטַיֵּיל אַחֲרָיו עַד שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְעִירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues after the refusal in step 3; רבי אלעזר keeps trying to make peace.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The townspeople ask the man to forgive for the sake of the Torah's honor.

steps.title: The man forgives, with a condition
steps.stepSummary: The man forgives for the townspeople's sake, on condition that רבי אלעזר does not make a habit of acting this way.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'For your sake I forgive him, as long as he does not get used to doing this.'
steps.whatsHappening: The conflict is settled: the man forgives רבי אלעזר, but only because the townspeople asked, and with a warning attached.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The forgiveness does not erase what happened. It is given for the sake of others. The condition 'not to make a habit of it' shows the real aim is for him to change.

keyTerms.meaning: used to it, in the habit of

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: בִּשְׁבִילְכֶם הֲרֵינִי מוֹחֵל לוֹ,
phrases.english: He said to them: For your sake I hereby forgive him,

phrases.aramaic: וּבִלְבַד שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא רָגִיל לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן.
phrases.english: provided that he does not make a habit of doing this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם: בִּשְׁבִילְכֶם הֲרֵינִי מוֹחֵל לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the townspeople's request in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He forgives on condition that the behavior does not happen again.

steps.title: Be soft like a reed, not stiff like a cedar
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון turns his experience into a public lesson: be flexible and humble like a reed. That is why the reed was chosen to become the pen for writing Torah, תפילין and מזוזות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Right away רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון went in and taught: 'A person should always be soft like a reed and not hard like a cedar. That is why the reed earned the honor of becoming the quill used to write a ספר תורה, תפילין and מזוזות.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the lesson of the story. רבי אלעזר publicly teaches the humility he just learned the hard way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A reed bends with the wind, while a cedar stands stiff and proud. רבי אלעזר says the humble reed is rewarded: it becomes the quill used to write the holiest texts. Humility, not pride, makes a person a fitting tool for Torah.
steps.whatToRemember: The story teaches that even a great Torah scholar must never insult a person, especially about something he cannot control, like his looks. Humility (the reed) is the trait that makes a person worthy of Torah.
steps.whyThisMatters: The reed-and-cedar lesson is one of the best-known lessons about humility in חז״ל. It ties good character directly to being a 'vessel' for Torah.

phrases.aramaic: מִיָּד נִכְנַס רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, וְדָרַשׁ:
phrases.english: Immediately Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon went in and taught:
A person should always be soft like a reed
and should not be hard like a cedar.
And therefore the reed merited
that a quill is taken from it

phrases.aramaic: לִכְתּוֹב בּוֹ סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה תְּפִילִּין וּמְזוּזוֹת.
phrases.english: to write with it a Torah scroll, phylacteries and mezuzot.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִיָּד נִכְנַס רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, וְדָרַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the whole story into a lasting lesson.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Be humble and flexible like a reed, not proud like a cedar. Humility makes a person worthy of Torah.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: a city with plague or collapsing buildings
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה, about a city struck by plague or collapsing buildings, to begin explaining it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And likewise, a city that has plague or collapsing buildings, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story is over. The גמרא now returns to the משנה and quotes its next case to set up an explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a setup line. It quotes the משנה's case of דבר (plague) or מפולת (collapsing buildings). In that case the city fasts and sounds the alarm. The next step explains what kind of מפולת the משנה means.

keyTerms.meaning: etc.; short for 'and so on', meaning the rest of the line is assumed

phrases.english: And likewise, a city in which there is
plague or collapsing buildings, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' points to the rest of the משנה: that city fasts and sounds the alarm.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן עִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ דֶּבֶר אוֹ מַפּוֹלֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the story and returns to the next case in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city struck by plague or collapsing buildings fasts and sounds the alarm, as the משנה says.

steps.title: Which collapses count: sturdy walls, not weak ones
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא explains that the משנה's 'collapsing buildings' means strong walls that were not expected to fall, not weak walls that were ready to fall anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: The 'collapsing buildings' they spoke of means healthy walls, not shaky ones. That is, walls that were not ready to fall, not walls that were ready to fall.
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא defines the משנה's term מפולת. Only the collapse of strong, sound walls is a sign of trouble that calls for a fast.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a weak, crumbling wall falls, that is normal and expected, so there is no reason to fast. When sturdy walls fall for no clear reason, that is an unusual disaster, and it calls for a public response. The ברייתא gives two descriptions: 'sturdy, not shaky' and 'not ready to fall, not those ready to fall'. The next step asks why both are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: ready to fall, likely to fall

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's מפולת counts only when sturdy walls collapse unexpectedly. Weak walls falling is expected and is no reason to fast.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule: a public fast is called only for unusual disasters, not for natural, expected events.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: The collapsing buildings that they spoke of
means sturdy ones and not shaky ones,
ones that are not ready to fall,
and not ones that are ready to fall.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַפּוֹלֶת שֶׁאָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the term מפולת from the משנה quoted in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only the collapse of sturdy walls that were not likely to fall counts as the משנה's מפולת.

steps.title: Isn't the ברייתא repeating itself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא lists 'sound' and 'not ready to fall' separately, and 'weak' and 'ready to fall' separately, since each pair seems to mean the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are 'sound' walls? Aren't they just walls not ready to fall? What are 'weak' walls? Aren't they just walls ready to fall?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the ברייתא from step 8, which seems to say the same thing twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא described the walls that count as 'sound, not ready to fall', as opposed to 'weak, ready to fall'. If 'sound' always means 'not ready to fall', the second word in each pair adds nothing. So the גמרא wants to know what each extra description teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: Which are they? (here used to say: aren't these the same thing?)

phrases.english: Which are 'sound' walls?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is pointing out that the ברייתא seems to say the same thing twice.

phrases.english: They are the same as walls not ready to fall!
Which are 'weak' walls?
They are the same as walls ready to fall!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵי נִיהוּ בְּרִיאוֹת, הֵי נִיהוּ שֶׁאֵינָן רְאוּיוֹת לִיפּוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא quoted in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The double description in the ברייתא ('sound' plus 'not ready to fall'; 'weak' plus 'ready to fall').
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each pair seems to mean the same thing, so one word in each pair looks extra.

steps.title: Strong walls that fell because they were too tall
steps.stepSummary: The extra wording is needed for a wall that is strong but fell because it was very tall.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed for walls that fell because of their height.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a wall can be strong and still be 'ready to fall', as when it is built too tall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Sound' and 'not ready to fall' are not always the same. A well-built wall that is extremely tall is sound but still likely to fall. Its falling would not show a plague of collapsing buildings, so the ברייתא needs both words.

keyTerms.meaning: it is needed only for... (the case is needed to teach something)

phrases.english: No, it is needed
for walls that fell because of their height.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דִּנְפַלוּ מֵחֲמַת גּוּבְהַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining a case where the two words differ
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Sound' and 'not ready to fall' mean the same thing.
steps.terutzMaskana: A wall can be strong but still likely to fall because of its great height.

steps.title: Or: strong walls standing on a riverbank
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the wall is strong, but it stands on a riverbank where the ground is not stable.
steps.simpleTranslation: Alternatively, it means walls that stood on a riverbank.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second example of a strong wall that is still 'ready to fall'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the danger does not come from the wall at all but from its location. The riverbank can wash away, so even a well-built wall there is likely to fall.

phrases.english: Alternatively,
it means walls that were standing on a riverbank.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי נָמֵי, דְּקָיְימָן אַגּוּדָּא דְנַהֲרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the challenge of step 9.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only a weak wall is ready to fall.
steps.terutzMaskana: A strong wall on unstable ground by a river is also ready to fall.
steps.whatToRemember: 'Ready to fall' can describe a strong wall, either because it is very tall or because it stands on a riverbank. Such a wall falling does not show a plague of collapsing buildings.

steps.title: The weak wall in נהרדעא that רב and שמואל avoided
steps.stepSummary: Like the weak walls mentioned above, there was a weak wall in נהרדעא that רב and שמואל would never walk under, even though it had stood for thirteen years.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like that weak wall in נהרדעא that רב and שמואל would not pass under, even though it had stood in its place for thirteen years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story about a weak wall. This line sets the scene for what happens in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though the wall had lasted thirteen years, רב and שמואל still treated it as dangerous. A weak wall stays 'ready to fall' no matter how long it has stood.

phrases.english: Like that weak wall
that was in Neharde'a,

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא הֲוָה חָלֵיף רַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל תּוּתַהּ,
phrases.english: that Rav and Shmuel would not pass under,
even though it stood
in its place for thirteen years.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הַהִיא אֲשִׁיתָא רְעִיעֲתָא דַּהֲוַאי בִּנְהַרְדְּעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life example of a weak wall like the ones discussed in steps 8 to 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A weak wall is treated as dangerous even if it has stood for many years.

steps.title: No need to go around: רב אדא בר אהבה is with us
steps.stepSummary: When רב אדא בר אהבה came along, שמואל suggested going around the wall. רב said it was not needed, because רב אדא בר אהבה's great merit protected them.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day רב אדא בר אהבה came there. שמואל said to רב: Come, let us go around. רב said: We don't need to today, because רב אדא בר אהבה, whose merit is great, is with us, so I am not afraid.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. רב feels safe walking under the weak wall because a very righteous person is with them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally they avoided the wall. Here רב relies on the זכות of רב אדא בר אהבה to protect them from danger. This sets up the question, answered in steps 15 and 16, of whether one may rely on such protection.

phrases.english: One day there happened to come
Rav Adda bar Ahava, to there.
Shmuel said to Rav:
Come, master, let us go around!
He said to him: I don't need to now,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִיכָּא רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה בַּהֲדַן
phrases.english: since Rav Adda bar Ahava is with us,
whose merit is great,
phrases.notes: Some versions add the letter in square brackets. The meaning is the same either way.

phrases.english: and so I am not afraid.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד אִיקְּלַע רַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה לְהָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of the weak wall in נהרדעא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The great merit of a righteous person can protect the people with him from danger.

steps.title: רב הונא's wine and the house that collapsed
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא kept רב אדא בר אהבה busy learning inside a weak house until his wine was moved out. The house fell right after they left, and רב אדא בר אהבה was upset when he realized what had happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא had wine in a weak house and wanted to move it out. He brought רב אדא בר אהבה in there and kept him busy with a Torah discussion until it was cleared out. After he left, the house fell. רב אדא בר אהבה realized what had happened and was upset.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about רב אדא בר אהבה's merit protecting people from a weak building. This time he is upset about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא used רב אדא בר אהבה's merit on purpose, without telling him. The house falling right afterward shows that his merit really had held it up. His anger leaves us asking why he was upset, and the גמרא answers in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: to clear it out, move it
a Torah discussion, a halachic topic

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא חַמְרָא
phrases.english: Rav Huna had some wine
in a certain weak house,
and he wanted to move it out.

phrases.aramaic: עַיְּילֵיהּ לְרַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה לְהָתָם,
phrases.english: He brought Rav Adda bar Ahava in there,
and kept him busy with a Torah discussion until they had cleared it out.
After he left, the house fell.
Rav Adda bar Ahava realized what had happened
and became upset.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא חַמְרָא בְּהָהוּא בֵּיתָא רְעִיעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story showing רב אדא בר אהבה's protective merit, now with a negative reaction from him.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב אדא בר אהבה's merit held up the weak house, but he was upset that it had been used this way.

steps.title: Why he was upset: don't rely on miracles
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר אהבה follows רבי ינאי: never stand in danger counting on a miracle. It may not happen, and if it does, it is taken off your merits.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds like רבי ינאי, who said: A person should never stand in a dangerous place and say, 'A miracle will be done for me,' because maybe no miracle will be done for him. And even if a miracle is done for him, it is deducted from his merits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב אדא בר אהבה was upset, using a teaching of רבי ינאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two dangers in relying on a miracle. First, the miracle might not come. Second, even if it comes, it 'costs' some of your זכויות. רב אדא בר אהבה was upset because his merits were used up to save רב הונא's wine.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a lasting principle: a person may not put himself in danger and count on Heavenly protection, and even a miracle that does happen comes at a cost.

phrases.english: He holds like this teaching
that Rabbi Yannai said:

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם אַל יַעֲמוֹד אָדָם בְּמָקוֹם סַכָּנָה
phrases.english: A person should never stand in a place of danger
and say: 'A miracle will be done for me,'
because maybe no miracle will be done for him.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר עוֹשִׂין לוֹ נֵס —
phrases.english: And even if you say a miracle is done for him,
it is deducted from his merits.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָבַר לַהּ כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind רב אדא בר אהבה's anger in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Never rely on a miracle in a dangerous place. It may not come, and if it does, it is deducted from one's merits.

steps.title: The פסוק: 'I have become small from all the kindnesses'
steps.stepSummary: רב חנן supports רבי ינאי's teaching from יעקב's words, which show that receiving kindness from ה׳ lessens a person's merits.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנן said: What is the verse for this? As it is written: 'I have become small from all the kindnesses and from all the truth.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב חנן brings a פסוק to back up the idea that a miracle uses up a person's merits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יעקב says he has 'become small' because of all the kindness ה׳ did for him. רב חנן reads this to mean that each kindness reduced his זכויות. That matches רבי ינאי's point that miracles are 'paid for' out of one's merits.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the verse (that teaches this)?

steps.whatToRemember: The stories of רב אדא בר אהבה teach that a righteous person's merit can protect others. But according to רבי ינאי, relying on a miracle is dangerous and uses up one's זכויות, as hinted in יעקב's words 'קטנתי מכל החסדים'.

phrases.english: Rav Chanan said: What is the verse for this?
As it is written: 'I have become small from all the kindnesses
and from all the truth.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָנָן: מַאי קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides a source in a פסוק for רבי ינאי's teaching in step 15.
steps.raayaObject: רבי ינאי's teaching that a miracle is deducted from one's merits.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 32:11, where יעקב says 'קטנתי מכל החסדים ומכל האמת'.

steps.title: What were the special deeds of רב אדא בר אהבה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which deeds earned רב אדא בר אהבה the great merit described in the stories above.
steps.simpleTranslation: What were the deeds of רב אדא בר אהבה?
steps.whatsHappening: We just heard that רב אדא בר אהבה's merit was strong enough to protect people from a falling wall. Now the גמרא asks what he actually did to earn that merit, and this sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier stories showed that he had great merit but never said where it came from. This question moves the discussion from the protection itself to the deeds that earned it.

keyTerms.meaning: his deeds, the way he acted

phrases.english: What were the deeds
of רב אדא בר אהבה?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי הֲוָה עוֹבָדֵיהּ דְּרַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks where the merit came from that the earlier stories took for granted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which deeds gave רב אדא בר אהבה his great merit.

steps.title: רב אדא בר אהבה lists the habits that gave him long life
steps.stepSummary: His students asked how he lived so long. He listed his habits: he never got angry at home, always showed respect to greater people, guarded the honor of Torah, never slept in the בית המדרש, and was careful with his friends' feelings.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: his students asked רב אדא בר אהבה, 'How did you merit long life?' He said: In all my days I never got angry in my home. I never walked in front of someone greater than me. I never thought about Torah in filthy alleys. I never walked four אמות without Torah and without תפילין. I never slept in the בית המדרש, not a deep sleep and not a nap. I never rejoiced when my friends stumbled. I never called a friend by his nickname. Some say: by his family nickname.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting רב אדא בר אהבה himself. He lists the good habits he kept his whole life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list covers different parts of life: peace at home, respect for greater people, honor for Torah and the בית המדרש, and care for other people's feelings. These steady, everyday habits are what built the merit we saw in the stories.

keyTerms.meaning: I got angry, I was strict and short-tempered
a nickname, especially one that is a put-down

steps.whatToRemember: רב אדא בר אהבה's great merit came from small, steady habits of respect, peace and care for others, kept every day of his life.

phrases.english: As it was stated:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאֲלוּ תַּלְמִידָיו לְרַב אַדָּא בַּר אַהֲבָה:
phrases.english: His students asked רב אדא בר אהבה:
Through what did you merit long life?
He said to them:
In all my days I never got angry inside my home,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא צָעַדְתִּי בִּפְנֵי מִי שֶׁגָּדוֹל מִמֶּנִּי,
phrases.english: and I never walked in front of someone greater than me,
and I never thought in filthy alleys,
phrases.notes: He means he never thought about Torah in dirty places.

phrases.english: and I never walked four אמות
without Torah and without תפילין,
and I never slept in the בית המדרש,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שֵׁינַת קֶבַע וְלֹא שֵׁינַת עֲרַאי,
phrases.english: not a deep sleep and not a nap,
and I never rejoiced when my friends stumbled,
and I never called my friend by his nickname,
and some say: by his family nickname.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּאִתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 17.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: His lifelong habits of peace at home, respect, honor for Torah, never sleeping in the בית המדרש, and care for his friends.

steps.title: רב הונא had weak walls torn down and rebuilt
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks רפרם בר פפא about רב הונא's good deeds. רפרם tells him that on cloudy days רב הונא toured the city and had every weak wall torn down. The owner rebuilt it if he could afford it, and if not, רב הונא paid for it himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רפרם בר פפא: Please tell us some of the fine deeds רב הונא used to do. He answered: I don't remember his younger years, but I remember his old age. On every cloudy day they took him out in a golden carriage, and he toured the whole town. Every weak wall he had torn down. If the owner could afford it, the owner rebuilt it. If not, רב הונא built it himself with his own money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another story of a great person's good deeds. רב הונא made sure no weak wall would fall and hurt anyone, even paying for poor people's walls himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This ties back to the weak walls in the earlier stories. Instead of relying on merit or a miracle, רב הונא actively removed the danger. Cloudy days mattered because rain could make a weak wall collapse.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the right way to deal with danger, matching רבי ינאי's teaching: don't count on a miracle, remove the danger yourself.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַפְרָם בַּר פָּפָּא:
phrases.english: רבא said to רפרם בר פפא:
Let the master tell us
some of those fine deeds
that רב הונא used to do!
He said to him:
His younger years I don't remember,
his old age I do remember.
For on every cloudy day
they would take him out in a golden carriage,
and he would inspect the whole town.
And every wall that was weak,
he would have it torn down.
If its owner could afford it, the owner rebuilt it,
and if he could not,
רב הונא himself built it with his own money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא לְרַפְרָם בַּר פָּפָּא לֵימָא לַן מָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רב אדא בר אהבה's deeds to רב הונא's deeds, again connected to weak walls.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא removed the danger of weak walls and paid for rebuilding when the owner could not.

steps.title: רב הונא bought the leftover vegetables every Friday
steps.stepSummary: Every Friday afternoon רב הונא sent a messenger to the market to buy all the vegetables the gardeners had not sold, and then threw them into the river.
steps.simpleTranslation: Every Friday afternoon he sent a messenger to the market. All the vegetables the gardeners had left over, he bought and threw into the river.
steps.whatsHappening: רפרם tells another good deed of רב הונא: he bought up all the unsold vegetables before שבת. The surprising part is that he threw them away, which the גמרא will question next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Buying the leftovers meant the gardeners did not lose money on produce they could not sell. The next steps explain why he threw the vegetables away instead of using them.

phrases.english: And every Friday afternoon
he would send a messenger to the market,
and all the vegetables
that the gardeners had left over,
he would buy
and throw into the river.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second good deed of רב הונא told by רפרם.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא bought all unsold vegetables before שבת and threw them into the river.
steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֹל פַּנְיָא דְּמַעֲלֵי שַׁבְּתָא הֲוָה מְשַׁדַּר שְׁלוּחָא לְשׁוּקָא

steps.title: Why not give the vegetables to the poor?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: instead of throwing the vegetables away, he should have given them to poor people.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him give them to the poor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the story: throwing away good food seems wasteful when poor people could eat it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the goal was only to help the gardeners, he could have helped the poor at the same time. So why waste the food?

phrases.english: But let him give them to the poor!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיתְּבֵיהּ לַעֲנִיִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's action of throwing the vegetables away.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's practice of throwing the vegetables into the river.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Giving the food to the poor would be a double good deed and would not waste food.

steps.title: The poor would stop buying vegetables
steps.stepSummary: If the poor knew they would get free vegetables, they would sometimes rely on that and not come to buy, which would hurt the gardeners.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sometimes they would rely on it and not come to buy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that giving the vegetables to the poor would backfire. The poor would wait for the free food instead of buying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Then the gardeners would sell even less, which defeats the whole purpose of helping them. Throwing the vegetables away kept the market working normally.

keyTerms.meaning: they rely on it, they count on it

phrases.english: Sometimes they would rely on it
and not come to buy.
phrases.notes: The poor would wait for רב הונא's free vegetables, so the gardeners would lose customers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reason: the suggestion would cause harm.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Giving to the poor seemed like a better use of the food.
steps.terutzMaskana: It would make the poor stop buying and hurt the gardeners' sales.
steps.triggerLanguage: זִמְנִין דְּסָמְכָא דַּעְתַּיְיהוּ וְלָא אָתוּ לְמִיזְבַּן

steps.title: Why not feed the vegetables to animals?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks again: if not to the poor, he could at least have thrown the vegetables to animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him throw them to the animals!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again: feeding animals would not hurt the market, so why waste the food in the river?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Animals would not stop anyone from buying, so the reason from the last step does not apply here. The question is why he still chose the river.

phrases.english: But let him throw them to the animals!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִשְׁדְּיֵיהּ לִבְהֵמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge, now that giving to the poor has been ruled out.
steps.kashyaTarget: Throwing the vegetables into the river.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Feeding animals would not hurt the gardeners, so there is no reason to waste the food.

steps.title: Human food may not be fed to animals
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא held that food meant for people should not be fed to animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that we do not feed human food to animals.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב הונא held a rule against giving people's food to animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Feeding human food to animals treats it with disrespect. So he could not use the animal option, and throwing the vegetables away was the only choice left.

keyTerms.meaning: he holds, this is his opinion

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא bought leftover vegetables to protect the gardeners' income. He did not give them to the poor, because then they would stop buying. He did not feed them to animals, because human food should not be given to animals.

phrases.english: He holds:
Human food may not be fed to animals.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Halachic principle held by רב הונא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Feeding animals seemed harmless and not wasteful.
steps.terutzMaskana: Feeding human food to animals is not allowed in his view, so the river was the only option.
steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: מַאֲכַל אָדָם אֵין מַאֲכִילִין לִבְהֵמָה

steps.title: Why buy the vegetables at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the vegetables could not go to the poor or to animals, the גמרא asks why רב הונא bought them in the first place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then he should not have bought them at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes a third challenge in this series. If the vegetables just end up in the river, why should רב הונא buy them?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 21–24 ruled out giving the vegetables to the poor or to animals. Since the vegetables are wasted either way, it seems pointless to spend money on them.

phrases.english: Then he should not buy them at all!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא לִיזְבְּנֵיהּ כְּלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the answer in step 24. Since no good use for the vegetables is left, it questions buying them at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's practice of buying the unsold vegetables (step 20)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the bought vegetables are only thrown away, the purchase seems to have no purpose.

steps.title: Buying them protects the future supply
steps.stepSummary: If the sellers are left with unsold produce, they will bring less next time, and people will be short of food for שבת.
steps.simpleTranslation: You would be found causing them to stumble in the future.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that buying the vegetables protects next week's market.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The purchase is not about using the vegetables. It shows the gardeners that everything they bring gets sold. If they had leftovers, they would bring less the next Friday, and people would not have enough for שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: in the future (here: the coming weeks)

steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא bought the leftovers so the sellers would keep bringing enough for שבת. He threw them away because giving them to the poor would hurt sales, and feeding people's food to animals is not respectful.
steps.confusionAlert: Here לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא does not mean עולם הבא. It simply means the coming weeks.

phrases.english: You would be found causing them to stumble in the future.
phrases.notes: If he didn't buy them, the sellers would bring less next Friday, and people would be short for שבת.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִמְצֵאתָ מַכְשִׁילָן לֶעָתִיד לָבֹא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the hidden purpose behind the purchase
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Buying vegetables only to throw them away is pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The purchase keeps the sellers from cutting back their supply for future weeks.

steps.title: רב הונא's free medicine at the door
steps.stepSummary: When רב הונא had a medicine, he filled a jug with it, hung it at his doorway, and invited anyone who needed it to take some.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he had a medicine, he would fill a jug with it, hang it at the doorway of his house, and say: Whoever needs it, let him come and take.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new kind act of רב הונא: sharing medicine with anyone who needed it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds another example of רב הונא's generosity. He did not wait for people to ask. He made the medicine easy to reach at his door.

phrases.english: When he had a medicine,
he would fill a jug with it,
phrases.notes: Some versions say "a jug of water." The corrected wording, in square brackets, says he filled the jug with the medicine itself.

phrases.english: and hang it at the doorway of the house,
and say: Whoever needs, let him come and take.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הֲוָה לֵיהּ מִילְּתָא דְאָסוּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the vegetable discussion and adds another good habit of רב הונא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא openly shared his medicine with anyone who needed it.

steps.title: Another version: water against the spirit שיבתא
steps.stepSummary: Others say רב הונא knew a remedy against the harmful spirit שיבתא. He hung up a jug of water and invited anyone who needed it to come in, so they would not be in danger.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: He knew a remedy against שיבתא. He would set out a jug of water and hang it up, and say: Whoever needs, let him come in so that he will not be in danger.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the same story. In this version, the jug at the door held water for protection, not medicine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the jug held medicine. In this version, it held water for protection against שיבתא. Either way, רב הונא used his own knowledge to help anyone who came.

phrases.english: And some say:
He knew by tradition a remedy against שיבתא,

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲוָה מַנַּח כּוּזָא דְמַיָּא וְדָלֵי לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: and he would set out a jug of water and hang it up,
and say: Whoever needs —
let him come in, so that he will not be in danger.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Retells step 27's story in a different way.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, רב הונא offered water at his door to protect people from שיבתא.

steps.title: רב הונא's open door at meals
steps.stepSummary: Whenever רב הונא sat down to eat, he opened his doors and invited anyone in need to come and eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he would eat bread, he would open his doors and say: Whoever needs, let him come and eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells of another kind habit of רב הונא. He opened his home to the hungry at every meal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the kindness goes further than leaving something outside. He let needy people into his home to eat with him. This habit is what רבא is about to call too hard for himself.

keyTerms.meaning: to eat a meal (literally: wrap bread)

phrases.english: When he would eat bread,
he would open his doors,
and say: Whoever needs,
let him come and eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הֲוָה כָּרֵךְ רִיפְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of רב הונא's generous habits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב הונא invited anyone in need to eat with him at every meal.

steps.title: רבא can follow all except one
steps.stepSummary: רבא says he can keep all of רב הונא's habits except one. His sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: I can keep all of them, except for this one, which I am not able to do,
steps.whatsHappening: רבא reacts to the list of רב הונא's habits. This line sets up his explanation on the next amud of which habit he cannot keep and why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא admits that one habit is beyond him. The words "this one" seem to point to the habit just mentioned, opening the doors at meals. His reason comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: רבא said:
All of them I am able to keep,
phrases.notes: "All of them" means all of רב הונא's habits that the גמרא just listed.

phrases.english: except for this one, which I am not able to do,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא כּוּלְּהוּ מָצֵינָא מְקַיַּימְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא reacts to the habits listed in steps 27–29 and singles out one as too hard for him.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא can follow all of רב הונא's habits except one, and his reason is given on the next amud.
